content: 1. The management of tuberculosis (TB) and HIV co-infection is critical, as outlined in Chapter 6. Excluding HIV co-infection simplifies the clinical diagnosis of TB, as HIV can complicate the presentation and progression of TB. 2. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients, including children, who are either suspected of having TB or have been diagnosed with TB. This is a strong recommendation, although the quality of evidence is low, as per the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on collaborative TB/HIV activities. 3. HIV testing is particularly recommended for all children being evaluated for TB or those diagnosed with TB in settings where HIV is endemic or in populations at high risk for HIV infection. 4. A systematic approach to diagnosing TB in children includes taking a detailed history, including exposure to TB contacts and symptoms consistent with TB. Close contact with a source case, especially one with sputum smear-positive TB, significantly increases the likelihood of transmission. 5. In children under 5 years of age, the source of TB infection is often a household contact. Infants and young children are particularly vulnerable to contracting TB at home. The development of TB in children typically occurs within one year of exposure and infection. 6. All children aged 0–4 years, regardless of symptoms, and children aged 5 years and older who are symptomatic and have been in close contact with a TB case, must be evaluated for TB. Additionally, all children living with HIV who have been in close contact with a TB case must also be evaluated. 7. When a child is diagnosed with TB, efforts should be made to identify the source case (if not already identified) and any other undiagnosed cases within the household. 8. Children with infectious TB, such as sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB or cavitary TB on chest X-ray, should be considered infectious. This is more common in older children and adolescents. 9. Common symptoms of TB in children include cough, fever, poor appetite or anorexia, weight loss or failure to thrive, fatigue, reduced playfulness, and decreased activity levels. Growth charts should be reviewed to assess weight loss or failure to thrive. 10. Certain physical signs are highly suggestive of extrapulmonary TB, such as a gibbous deformity (indicative of vertebral TB) or non-painful enlarged cervical lymphadenopathy with or without fistula formation. Other signs, such as meningitis unresponsive to antibiotics, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, ascites, or non-painful enlarged joints, warrant further investigation for TB. 11. A tuberculin skin test (TST) is a useful tool for assessing TB infection in children, especially when there is no known history of TB contact. A positive TST indicates prior or current infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but it does not confirm active TB disease. It should be used alongside other diagnostic tests. 12. False-positive TST results can occur due to prior Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, while false-negative results may occur in HIV-positive children, those with severe TB disease, or malnourished children. A negative TST does not rule out TB infection or disease. 13. Bacteriological confirmation of TB should be pursued whenever possible by obtaining appropriate specimens for microscopy, culture, and histopathological examination. Culture is more likely to yield a positive diagnosis in children, as TB in this population is often paucibacillary. 14. Bacteriological confirmation is particularly important in cases of suspected drug-resistant TB, HIV co-infection, severe or complicated TB, uncertain diagnoses, or in children who have been previously treated for TB. 15. Chest radiography is a valuable diagnostic tool for pulmonary TB in children. Common findings include persistent lung opacification with enlarged hilar or subcarinal lymph nodes. A miliary pattern of opacification is highly suggestive of TB in HIV-negative children. 16. Adolescents with TB often present with radiographic changes similar to adults, such as large pleural effusions, apical infiltrates with cavity formation, or primary disease with hilar adenopathy and collapse lesions. 17. Good-quality chest radiographs, including lateral views when possible, are essential for proper evaluation and should be interpreted by trained radiologists or healthcare workers. 18. Extrapulmonary TB in children is often suspected based on clinical presentation and confirmed through histology or specialized investigations. All fluid samples (e.g., cerebrospinal, pleural, ascitic, joint, or pericardial) should undergo biochemical analysis, cell count, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining, and culture whenever possible. 19. Fine-needle aspiration of enlarged lymph nodes for AFB staining, culture, and histology has shown high diagnostic yield and is particularly useful in pediatric TB cases. 20. Molecular diagnostic tools, such as the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, are increasingly used for rapid detection of TB and rifampicin resistance in children. These tools are particularly valuable in resource-limited settings. 21. The WHO does not currently recommend the routine use of scoring systems for diagnosing TB in children, as these systems have shown poor and variable performance, especially in pulmonary TB and HIV-positive children. 22. The treatment of TB in children follows the same principles as in adults, with the primary objectives being to cure the patient, prevent death, avoid relapse, reduce transmission, and minimize drug resistance and toxicity. 23. Recommended daily dosages of anti-TB medications for children include isoniazid (10 mg/kg, range 7–15 mg/kg), rifampicin (15 mg/kg, range 10–20 mg/kg), pyrazinamide (35 mg/kg, range 30–40 mg/kg), and ethambutol (20 mg/kg, range 15–25 mg/kg). Dosages should be adjusted for young children due to differences in drug metabolism.
